question: Recent incidents of child abuse in Greece, with video recordings and physical attacks between schoolchildren, have highlighted the seriousness of school bullying in the country.

Correspondingly, the suicide of a 14-year-old in Italy after homophobic bullying, as well as cases in France (Lucas, 13 years old, Nicolas, 15 years old), Finland and the United Kingdom, demonstrate that the phenomenon constitutes an existential threat to the mental health and lives of minors in Europe.

The Charter of Fundamental Rights (Articles 7, 21, 24) guarantees the right to dignity, the prohibition of discrimination and the protection of the child. Regulation (EU) 2021/817 on Erasmus+ promotes inclusion and mental health, while Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act) strengthens the responsibility of platforms against cyberbullying.
At the same time, the EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child (2021) sets guidelines, but uneven implementation and the lack of binding mechanisms leave children exposed. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission intend to support Member States with binding guidelines, training and support structures for schools and teachers?
How will the Commission ensure that schools in rural or less developed areas have equal access to bullying prevention tools, resources and programmes?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.12.2025) The protection and empowerment of children online is a top priority for the Commission, as highlighted by the Commission President in the latest State of the Union address.

The Digital Services Act (DSA) establishes strong safeguards for minors online, complemented by the Better Internet for Kids+ Strategy that strives to ensure that every child is respected, protected and empowered online, and the EU Strategy on the Rights of the Child. In July 2025, the Commission adopted guidelines under the DSA to ensure high levels of privacy, safety and security for minors.

The Commission plans to adopt an EU Action Plan against Cyberbullying to tackle online abuse by defining cyberbullying at EU level and promoting prevention, awareness, empowerment, reporting, and victim support. These efforts align with the 2024 Recommendation on integrated child protection1, which calls on Member States to adopt comprehensive anti-bullying strategies.

Examples on how the Commission supports policymakers and educators include: guidelines on well-being and mental health at school2, the Digital Education Action Plan3 which promote digital skills and safe online behaviour. Moreover, the Commission co-funds Safer Internet Centres and their helplines—where cyberbullying is the top concern— showing the Commission’s strong track record.

Also, Erasmus+, the Citizenship, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV) programme, and the European Solidarity Corps fund initiatives that help educators, policymakers and young people address bullying. The initiatives above are EU-wide, and many of their tools and frameworks can be adapted to rural and less developed settings.
